title: Inventory, managed settings and spend ceilings

story: Ronen, who leads our security work, is filling in a customer's security review. One question asks for every AI system that can touch our code or data: what it sees, what it can change, and who owns it. He asks in Slack. Nave, who maintains Byte, our review agent, starts to collect the answer: the GitHub App's list of installed repos, three secrets in the org's Actions settings, the #byte channel, an account at a second model vendor. For Vanil, his compliance agent, the answer is in the credential store of n8n, the older workflow tool Vanil runs on, and only he can open it.

Two days later the answer is a long Slack thread, and it is already wrong, because someone installed Byte on one more repo in the meantime. Next month more agents join: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent; the routines, which are Nova started by events such as a red build; and a brain bot that answers questions in Slack. Each of them needs the same question answered before it gets a single permission.
hook.question: Where do we write down what each agent may touch, so that there is one answer, and it stays true?

read.h: One file, one row per agent
p: The answer is a file in the platform repo, inventory/agents.yaml, with one row for every AI agent we run or plan to run. A row says what the agent does, which model and vendors it uses, what data it sees, where its keys live, who owns it, and the exact repos, Jira issues and Slack channels it may use. It also says whether the agent runs unattended, which means that no person approves each run. The file holds no secrets, only the names of keys and where they are kept, so anyone who reviews it can read it.

The two live agents come first, because their access already exists and the file must describe the truth before it describes a plan. Byte's row is copied from Byte's own configuration, its model setting and its list of repos, not written from memory. It names two vendors: Anthropic for the review itself, and TypeSafe, an outside company whose model, Jev, Byte uses for a cheap first check on each new push. Where nobody is sure of a value yet, such as the exact model Vanil uses today, the row says so in a comment instead of guessing.

code.text:
# Every AI agent and exactly what it may touch. Changes are PRs reviewed by Security.
- name: byte
  status: live
  owner: nave
  does: advisory PR reviews, sniff, fix mode
  model: claude-opus-5-5, effort high              # byte src/engines.ts
  vendors: [anthropic, typesafe]
  data: diffs and comments of PRs in installed repos; no PHI
  keys: [BYTE_GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY, BYTE_CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, BYTE_TYPESAFE_API_KEY]   # org Actions secrets
  github: { app: byte-review, repos: installation roster, writes: [COMMENT reviews, fix PRs into the author's branch] }
  slack: ["#byte"]
  unattended: true

notes.text: The rule for the whole file: every change to an agent's access is a pull request that Security reviews.
Copied from Byte's own code, and the comment says where, so the next reader can check it.
Every vendor that sees our data is listed, not only the main one.
What data the agent sees. Every row says no PHI, patient data, because no agent may see it.
The names of the keys and where they live, never their values.
Byte reviews on its own: no person approves each run.

read.h: The narrowest row that still works
p: For a planned agent you write the row before the agent exists, and you write the narrowest set that still lets it do its job. For Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, that is one repo, fcp; a GitHub token from the broker, our service that holds the GitHub, Jira and Slack credentials and makes those calls for a run, that can write code and pull requests in that one repo for one hour; the Jira issue it was assigned; and the Slack thread for that ticket. Its keys line says none in the VM, the fresh machine each run works on, because the broker holds those credentials and the LLM gateway, the service that adds the Anthropic key to each model call, holds that key. Routines, which are Nova started by an event and run unattended, get one more rule: no Jira writes beyond their own ticket, because nobody watches each run.

This is the principle of least privilege, applied row by row: give each agent the smallest access that still does the job, so that a mistake, or an agent fooled by text it read, can only do small damage. Writing the row first has a second effect. The broker's scopes and the routines' charters, the written rules each routine works under, are built to grant what the row says and nothing more. A wider permission later starts as a change to this file.

code.text:
- name: nova
  status: planned
  owner: sean
  model: routing table, Opus 5.5 at medium by default
  vendors: [anthropic (ZDR org, workspace nova)]
  data: fcp code and fake seed data only; no PHI
  keys: none in the VM; the broker holds GitHub, Jira and Slack; the gateway holds Anthropic
  github: { app: rhino-ai-agents, repos: [fcp], token: "contents and pull_requests write, 1 h, one repo" }
  jira: the assigned issue only
  slack: the ticket's thread only
  unattended: false                                # one person approves the plan, a different one the PR

notes.text: planned tells the reader this row is a decision, not yet a running system.
Nova's key is in its own workspace of the agents' Anthropic organization, so its spend and its off switch are separate.
Nothing on the machine: the broker and the gateway hold every credential.
One App, one repo, a one-hour token that can write code and pull requests only.
Not unattended: a person approves the plan, and a different person approves the PR.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the same idea for models
p: The inventory says what each agent may touch. A second small file says which Claude Code features are off for everyone, people and agents alike. It is a managed settings file: settings the organization sets and a person cannot override, as in the lesson on hooks and managed settings. Ours, settings/managed-settings.d/10-models.json, changes two things and nothing else. deniedModels: ["fable"] hides the Fable models, because Fable needs 30 days of data retention, a compliance decision we have not made, and it is not available in the agents' zero-data-retention organization. CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS set to 0 keeps agent teams, an experimental feature where several sessions work as one team, switched off. It deliberately sets no model and no effort, so people keep Anthropic's defaults.

The same file reaches people and agents by two roads. For people, an admin pastes it into the claude.ai admin settings, and Claude Code downloads it when the person signs in. Agents never sign in to claude.ai; they reach Claude through the gateway, and sessions like that do not receive server-managed settings, so the VM image copies the file to /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.d/. On a laptop, /status lists the managed source and /model shows Fable hidden or greyed out. deniedModels needs Claude Code v2.1.283 or later.

read.h: Every change is a pull request
p: After the first review, nobody changes an agent's access in a console or in a chat message. A new channel for the brain bot, a second repo for a routine, a new vendor for Byte: each one is a pull request to this file, and Security reviews it. That is one file to review instead of five systems, and the history of the file is the history of every agent's access, with the reason and the reviewer next to each change.

Review rules that are written down can also be checked by a program. The lab turns four of them into tests that run on every pull request to the file: every agent has an owner, no agent sees PHI, a planned agent holds no keys in its VM, and a planned agent works in exactly one repo. A test like this does not replace the Security review. It catches the plain mistakes, so the reviewer can spend their time on the questions only a person can answer, such as whether a routine really needs a channel. The same kind of test can also compare a live row with the agent's real configuration, so a row that no longer matches reality fails the next pull request instead of waiting for someone to notice.

code.file: rules.test.ts (the lab's test, not a platform file)

notes.text: parse from the yaml package turns the file into plain objects, one per row.
Most rules are about planned agents, whose access we decide; live rows describe what already exists.
The keys rule from Nova's row, as an exact string, so a row that explains why it needs a key still fails.
One repo per planned agent. Work in a second repo is a person's decision, not a wider row.

✖ a planned agent holds no keys in its VM

deeper.h: Go deeper: spend limits that never cut a run
p: A third file, settings/spend-limits.yaml, holds the money rules, and they follow one principle: see spend before you limit it. No limit may stop a run in the middle, so every limit is far away, starts in shadow mode, which means it only logs what it would have done, for four weeks, and is set from real data. People see their own spend with /usage and the status line, and nobody sees a list of other people's spend. The shared R&D budget gets alerts at 50, 75 and 95 percent, and no person gets a cap until there are weeks of real numbers.

Each agent workspace, its own part of the agents' Anthropic organization with its own key, gets a monthly limit far above its expected spend, about three times, with alerts at 50, 75 and 90 percent. The one setting that ever acts is hold_new_runs_above_pct: 90. Above 90 percent of a workspace's limit, the orchestrator, the service that starts every run, lets running work finish and makes new runs wait in the queue. Holding a run that has not started costs a delay; cutting one that has started throws its work away.

lab.title: Answer Security's question from one file
lab.goal: Write a small agent inventory, answer "which agents can touch this repo?" from it in one command, and turn Security's review rules into tests that catch a row that is too wide.

guess.q: The bug fixer, a routine that runs unattended, asks for fcp and also the infrastructure repo, "in case the bug is there". Security's rule is one repo per planned agent. What should its row say?

options.text: Both repos, with a comment that explains why.
options.why: A comment does not make the access smaller. A fooled bug fixer could then change our cloud setup, with nobody watching the run.

options.text: No repos, so it asks a person for access each time.
options.why: Then it cannot do its job at all. The narrowest row still has to work.

options.text: Only fcp. A bug that lives in another repo goes to a person.
options.why: The rare case does not widen the row. A person can fix it, or open a reviewed change to the file if it keeps happening.

lab.build: Write a fifth rule in rules.test.ts: an unattended planned agent writes in Jira only on its own ticket, so its jira line must be none or its own ticket only. Run the tests and see the bug fixer fail it too. Then narrow the two rows until all five tests pass: cifix holds no keys in its VM, and the bug fixer gets one repo and Jira writes on its own ticket only. Finish by asking node who.ts RhinoHealth/infrastructure again.
checks: Before you fix the rows, the new rule fails with: bug-fixer has jira: comment on and move any RH ticket.
After the fix, node --test --test-reporter=spec rules.test.ts shows 5 tests, 5 pass and 0 fail.
node who.ts RhinoHealth/infrastructure says no agent can touch RhinoHealth/infrastructure.
node who.ts RhinoHealth/fcp still lists four agents, so nobody lost the access they need.
lab.fix: Last week someone added the brain's repo to Byte's own configuration, and nobody opened a pull request to the inventory. Make the lab copy of that configuration with echo '{ "repositories": ["RhinoHealth/fcp", "RhinoHealth/rnd-kb"] }' > byte-repositories.json and ask node who.ts RhinoHealth/rnd-kb. It says no agent can touch it, and every test still passes: the most dangerous kind of wrong answer. Write a test that compares Byte's repos with that file (sort both lists and use assert.deepEqual), see it fail, and then say which file should change, who reviews that change, and why deleting the new test is not the fix.
explain: Why is one reviewed file a better answer to "what may this agent touch" than asking the people who run each system?
Why do the live rows come first, and why are they copied from each agent's own configuration?
The bug fixer would sometimes be useful in a second repo. Why does its row still get exactly one?
lab.done: All five rules pass on the fixed inventory, who.ts says no agent can touch the infrastructure repo, and you can show the failing test that catches Byte's row drifting from its real configuration.

check.q: The brain bot needs one more Slack channel. What is the right first step?

options.text: Add the channel in Slack now and update the inventory later.
options.why: Then the file is wrong from the start, and the next person who asks gets an old answer. The file changes first.

options.text: Open a pull request that adds the channel to the brain bot's row, and ask Security to review it.
options.why: Every access change is a reviewed change to the one file. The systems then grant what the row says.

options.text: Ask in the team channel whether anyone objects.
options.why: A chat message leaves no reviewed record next to the access, and Security may never see it.

check.q: Why does the inventory describe the live agents, Byte and Vanil, before it describes the planned ones?

options.text: Because their access already exists, so the file must match reality before it can be trusted for anything new.
options.why: A file that is wrong about today's agents gives wrong answers from the first day. Copying the live rows from real configuration makes it true first.

options.text: Because the planned agents are not allowed to have rows until they are running.
options.why: The opposite: a planned agent's row is written first, and the systems are built from it.

options.text: Because the order of the rows decides which agent the broker checks first.
options.why: The order has no meaning to any program. It is about getting the facts right before the plans.

check.q: A routine's draft row lists two repos "in case the problem is in the second one". What does least privilege say?

options.text: Keep both, because a routine that cannot reach the problem is useless.
options.why: It can still do its job in the one repo. The rare case goes to a person.

options.text: Keep both, but only during the pilot weeks.
options.why: Access that is meant to be temporary usually stays. If it is really needed later, a reviewed change can add it then.

options.text: One repo, the one its job needs; anything else goes to a person or to a reviewed change of the file later.
options.why: The smallest access that still does the job keeps the damage small when the routine makes a mistake or is fooled.

p: G0-10 creates inventory/agents.yaml in RhinoHealth/ai-agents with Byte and Vanil (live) and Nova, the routines, the brain bot and the eval runner (planned). Byte's row is filled from byte's src/engines.ts and config/repositories.json, Vanil's from its n8n credentials with Nave. Ronen reviews the first version, and every later access change is a PR to this file reviewed by Security. G3's broker scopes and G5's routine charters read from it.

G0-12 adds settings/managed-settings.d/10-models.json (deniedModels fable, CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=0), pasted into claude.ai Admin Settings for people and baked into G3's Packer image at /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.d/ for agents. G0-16 turns on spend visibility, sets R&D pool alerts at 50, 75 and 95 percent, gives each ZDR workspace a monthly limit of about 3 times expected spend with alerts to #ai-agents-alerts, books 18 Nov (W7) with Ronen to set the per-person extra-usage limit from real data (first guess about $500), and writes settings/spend-limits.yaml, whose hold_new_runs_above_pct the orchestrator reads.

Still open in the plan: the inventory in the ticket mixes data with sentences (repos: installation roster; keys: none in the VM; the broker holds ...), but G3 and G5 are meant to read it, so the fields they read need a fixed, machine-readable shape. No ticket adds a CI check on the file (shape, the narrowest-row rules) or keeps the live rows in sync with Byte's config and Vanil's n8n credentials, so drift is only caught by people. Nova's row in the ticket should also say no PHI, as the live rows do.

tickets.why: The inventory: the live rows from real config, the narrowest planned rows, Security's review.
The managed-settings file from the first deeper panel: Fable denied, agent teams off, two roads.
The spend limits from the second deeper panel: shadow first, far away, hold new runs above 90 percent.

words.plain: One reviewed file with a row for every AI agent: what it does, what it sees, who owns it, and exactly what it may touch.
An agent that works without a person approving each run, such as Byte or a routine.
Give each agent the smallest access that still lets it do its job.
Claude Code settings the organization sets for everyone; a person cannot override them.
A limit that only logs what it would have done, for weeks, before it is allowed to act.

review.q: List what a row in the inventory says about an agent.
review.a: What it does, its model and vendors, the data it sees (no PHI), where its keys live (names only), its owner, the exact repos, Jira issues and Slack channels, and whether it runs unattended.

review.q: Write Nova's narrowest row from memory: repo, token, Jira, Slack, keys.
review.a: fcp only; a one-hour broker token with contents and pull_requests write in that one repo; the assigned issue only; the ticket's thread only; no keys in the VM (broker and gateway hold them).

review.q: Why does a hold on new runs fit our rules when a cap on running ones does not?
review.a: No limit may cut a run in the middle. Holding a run that has not started only delays it; cutting a running one throws its work away.

remember: One reviewed file says exactly what each agent may touch, in the narrowest row that still works, and every change to it is a pull request that Security reviews.
